Optimal policies

One policy is better than another if it gets at least as much expected return from every state. An optimal policy is one that no other policy beats anywhere. It can be read straight off the optimal action values: in each state, pick the action with the largest one.

The icy gridworld again. Every arrow starts pointing left, a poor policy. Click a cell to turn its arrow. Each cell shows its arrow and $v_\pi(s)$ for the whole policy. An amber frame means another action has a higher $q_\pi(s, a)$ there; the small amber arrow is that action.

Change the world

The optimal policy depends on the world. Press "Jump to optimal" and look at $(1,3)$, the cell left of 🕳️: it points ←, backing away, because going ↑ slides into the pit 10% of the time. Lower the slip to 0.15, or set the step reward to −1, and press "Jump to optimal" again: the arrow flips to ↑. Less risk, or a costlier detour, makes the direct route worth it. With slip 0, the best route is simply the shortest.

The maths

Policies are compared state by state:

$$\pi \ge \pi' \iff v_\pi(s) \ge v_{\pi'}(s) \text{ for all } s$$

Two policies need not be comparable: each could win in different states. Even so, for any finite MDP there is at least one policy $\pi_*$ that is $\ge$ every other. All optimal policies share the same value functions:

$$v_*(s) = \max_\pi v_\pi(s), \qquad q_*(s, a) = \max_\pi q_\pi(s, a)$$

$v_*(s)$ is the most expected return any policy can get from $s$. $q_*(s, a)$ is the most it can get after taking $a$ first. Once you have $q_*$, an optimal policy is greedy with respect to it:

$$\pi_*(s) = \arg\max_a q_*(s, a)$$

Taking the best first action and then behaving optimally is optimal, so

$$v_*(s) = \max_a q_*(s, a)$$

This is Lesson 23's average with all the weight on the best action. Ties in the argmax are fine: any action that reaches the maximum is optimal.

"Act greedily" uses the current policy's $q_\pi$, not $q_*$. Each press makes no cell worse and, while any amber frame remains, makes some cell strictly better. When no arrow changes, the policy is greedy with respect to its own values, and that only happens at an optimal policy. Lessons 31 and 32 prove both facts (the policy improvement theorem and policy iteration).
